newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Blair attacks U.S. over global warming.
newsitem.headline: Blair attacks U.S. over global warming.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair launched a thinly veiled attack on the United States and Canada on Monday for failing to do enough to cut the greenhouse gases that cause global warming.

Speaking at the opening session of a United Nations conference taking stock of progress since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, Blair said Britain had delivered on its targets for reducing greenhouse gases.
"Some other countries cannot say the same, including some of the great industrialised nations.
"To them I say this: our targets will not be taken seriously by the poorer countries until the richer countries are meeting them," Blair said.
He named no names, but British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook spoke at the weekend of a cultural divide between Europe and the United States and Canada.

"Both of them find it very difficult to deal with a domestic audience which is still very much in a culture of large, extravagant private cars and generous consumption of energy as a cheap commodity," Cook said during the annual summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations.
"The lifestyle of America and elsewhere cannot be contained much beyond another quarter of a century without serious effects on our climate," Cook said.

Blair committed Britain to cutting its emissions of carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas, by 20 percent from 1990 levels by 2010 and said sweeping lifestyle changes would be needed to hit the target.
New forms of energy would have to be promoted and greater use of public transport was essential.
To underline the scale of the political challenge, officials said that without further steps, carbon dioxide emissions in Britain by 2010 will be slightly higher than they were in 1990.

Blair ruled out at the weekend new environmental taxes but officials said the government was working on a broad range of measures to help meet the target -- including more bus lanes, energy efficiency schemes and improved traffic management.
Blair, who flew into New York from Denver on the fuel-hungry supersonic Concorde, suggested another energy-saving measure.
"Who knows whether a future Earth Summit might be done through tele and video-conferencing, with all of us staying at home?" he asked.
In another reference to North America, he said the biggest responsibility for tackling global warming lay with those countries with the biggest emissions.
"We in Europe have put our cards on the table. It is time for the special pleading to stop and for others to follow suit."
In a reference to a climate conference in Kyoto, Japan next December, he added: "If we fail in Kyoto, we fail our children, because the consequences will be felt in their lifetime.
"We must all deliver on the commitments we make. Setting new targets means little if old ones are ignored," he said.
